title: Simone Weil
keyWorks: “The Iliad, or the Poem of Force” (1940)
“Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)
summary: Simone Weil was a French philosopher, teacher and mystic who worked in a factory to understand the lives of workers and stood all her life on the side of those who struggle. Her central idea is attention: the ability to see reality and another person clearly, without the distortions of imagination. She wrote about the “gravity” of the soul and about “grace,” about the need for roots, and about how affliction wounds a person.
onEmotions: Weil described the life of the soul through the image of “gravity”: feelings pull us downward on their own, like a law of nature, and willpower alone is not enough. The opposite of gravity is “grace” — what comes as a gift. Imagination, in Weil's view, hurries to fill every void with comforting or frightening pictures; attention — patient, open, unstrained — brings us back to reality. She described “malheur” (affliction) — a fusion of pain and humiliation that leaves shame in the soul, as if the person were to blame. Her notion of “decreation” is not self-destruction (Weil herself distinguished the two) but loosening the ego's grip to make room for the world and for others.

anxiety.text: “Imagination, filler of the void,” Simone Weil once wrote. When we don't know what will happen, imagination hurries to complete the picture, often in the darkest colors — and the anxiety you feel is truly exhausting: your body is living in a future that doesn't exist yet. She saw “attention” as its opposite: the ability to stop and look at what is, without rushing to interpret it. Attention, for Weil, is not a strained effort but rather an open, patient waiting. For Weil, anxiety is imagination with nothing to lean on. You don't need to drive it away by force. You can gently bring your attention back to the present moment — to what is actually in front of you, not what fear has sketched in.
anxiety.practice: Hold one object — a key, a spoon, a pebble — and for three minutes look only at it, the way Weil advised looking at a problem: without hurrying to understand. When your mind runs into the future, bring it back to one detail.

fear.text: A refugee in wartime London, Simone Weil drafted a plan for France's rebirth for the Free French — and began it not with rights but with what the soul needs. She would not shame your fear: she took fear seriously. In The Need for Roots she drew up a list of the “needs of the soul” — things a person cannot fully live without, just as with food and sleep. One of them is security: a state in which the soul is not constantly weighed down by fear or terror. Yet she also named risk as a need — a meaningful encounter with danger that awakens courage. In this light, your fear is a signal of a real need, not a weakness. You might ask: what kind of security am I missing right now — and where could I find at least a little of it?
fear.practice: Look around the room and find three things protecting you right now: walls, a door, warm clothes. Name each one aloud — a small inventory of security, one of Weil's “needs of the soul.”

sadness.text: “Two forces rule the universe: light and gravity,” Simone Weil wrote. If you are being pulled down right now, it is not your fault. She described the life of the soul through the image of physical gravity: feelings, in her view, naturally sink downward, like a falling stone. This is not a reproach but an observation: this is how human nature works. The opposite of gravity she called “grace” — what comes not from our effort but as a gift, sometimes unexpectedly. For Weil, a believer, this was connected with God, but a reader without faith can understand her thought too: not everything that lifts us is something we can produce ourselves. Seen this way, sadness doesn't need to be overcome by a lunge of will. You can acknowledge its weight and remain open to what may come on its own.
sadness.practice: Lie down or sit so that your body gives itself fully to its weight — let gravity do its work. For a minute or two let it hold you, and notice where the sadness lives in your body.

quote.text: All the natural movements of the soul are controlled by laws analogous to those of physical gravity. Grace is the only exception.
quote.author: Simone Weil

grief.text: For Simone Weil, the hardest thing a soul can do is to leave an empty place empty. Your grief is an enormous pain, and there is no need to hurry it. She saw how hard it is to accept a void: the soul strives with all its might to fill it with something — imagined conversations, reproaches, fantasies of how things might have gone differently. Weil called such fillers “compensations.” She did not demand that we give them up through effort; she spoke of the courage to leave the place empty, at least for a while. Weil suggests that grief is love from which presence has been taken away. Love for someone absent, Weil believed, can be very pure: it no longer expects anything in return. Longing does not make your love smaller, and absence does not cancel what was.
grief.practice: Set out a cup or light a candle for the one who is gone, and sit beside it in silence for a minute, saying nothing and asking nothing of yourself. Let the place stay empty.

loneliness.text: In the Grail legend Weil loved, a knight heals a wounded king with a single question: “What are you going through?” When no one asks you that question, loneliness becomes especially heavy. For Simone Weil, attention to another person was the highest form of love. She wrote that true love of one's neighbor begins with a simple but very rare ability — to genuinely ask another person what they are going through, and to listen to the answer. It follows that loneliness is a hunger for that kind of attention. It is legitimate and does not make you weak. At the same time, Weil valued solitude: in silence, attention can grow deeper. Perhaps the first step is to give that attention to yourself, and the second is to look for people capable of it — or to give it to someone else.
loneliness.practice: Today, ask someone the Grail question — “How are you, really?” — and listen to the answer all the way through. If there's no one to ask, ask it of yourself aloud and wait in silence for the answer.

anger.text: In Le Puy, a young philosophy teacher named Simone Weil marched with the unemployed to the town hall, and the newspapers dubbed her “the Red Virgin”: she felt injustice in her body. Your anger has most likely met something unjust too, and Weil would take it seriously. In her essay “The Iliad, or the Poem of Force” she showed how violence turns a person into a thing — both the one it is aimed at and the one who wields it. She noticed that people tend to pass the pain done to them on to others. In other words, anger is legitimate, but its weight easily “spills over” onto others. Weil suggested keeping your attention on the injustice itself — seeing it clearly, without turning away — and not letting pain turn us into transmitters of force.
anger.practice: Clench your fists as hard as you like on an in-breath and slowly open them on the out-breath — the force passes through you but goes no further. Then name, in one phrase, the injustice your anger has seen.

shame.text: Weil noticed a strange thing: a person badly wounded by life is often ashamed of the wound, as if the blow had left not a scar but a brand. If shame is burning you now, it's worth asking where it came from. She described a particular state — “malheur,” usually translated as “affliction”: a fusion of pain, humiliation and social rejection. Weil noticed with remarkable precision that such affliction leaves a brand of shame and self-contempt on the soul, as though the person were to blame for what happened to them. Weil would probably say that shame is sometimes not the voice of conscience but the trace of a wound. It speaks of what happened to you, not of who you are. You can look at such shame with compassion rather than agreeing with it.
shame.practice: Place your palm where the shame burns most and quietly ask: “Is this about what I did, or about what was done to me?” Don't argue with the answer — just keep your hand there for a few more breaths.

guilt.text: “The notion of obligation comes before that of rights” — so begins Weil's The Need for Roots: first and foremost, we owe something to one another. If guilt is tormenting you, it means other people truly matter to you. Seen this way, guilt is a living sense of obligation. But Weil also noticed a trap: attention can quietly turn toward oneself — toward one's own image, toward the question “how bad am I?” Then guilt becomes a circle with “I” at its center once again. Carrying Weil's thought further, the way out is to bring your attention back to the person you feel guilty toward: what do they need now? In this way guilt turns from self-flagellation into care, and care can be expressed in a concrete act.
guilt.practice: Do one small concrete thing for the person you feel guilty toward — a message, a hand, a cup of tea — not to be forgiven but because they need it. Weil would call this turning attention from yourself to the other.

envy.text: Picture a hungry person at a shop window: the bread behind the glass looks brighter than anything they have. This, for Weil, is how the soul's “gravity” works, and she wouldn't shame the envy stinging you now. She wrote that the soul, feeling an inner emptiness, reaches for whatever might fill it — this is part of what she called “gravity.” For Weil, envy is a gaze fixed on the imagined fullness of someone else's life. We see in another what we lack and fill in the rest. Weil set attention to reality against imagination — including attention to your own life, just as it is. There is no need to be ashamed of envy; it shows what you want. But you can gently turn it around: not “why do they have that?” but “what in my own life have I not looked at attentively for a long time?”
envy.practice: Go for a five-minute walk and look only at what is yours: your street, your windows, your trees — as if seeing them for the first time. Find one thing in your own life you haven't looked at attentively in a long time.

emptiness.text: Weil once wrote: “Grace fills empty spaces, but it can only enter where there is a void to receive it.” When everything inside feels empty and nothing appeals, it is very heavy, and it is not laziness. In Simone Weil's writing the word “void” has an unusual meaning. She believed that the soul fears the void and hurries to fill it with anything at all — distractions, imagination, busyness. But in her view, it is precisely the void that can become the place where something new and real one day enters — what she called “grace.” This doesn't mean emptiness is pleasant or that you should seek it out. It means it is not necessarily final. From Weil's point of view, you need not fight emptiness with all your strength; you can let it be, like an empty place at the table where a guest may still arrive.
emptiness.practice: Pull one chair out from the table — an empty place where a guest may still arrive. Sit beside it for two minutes, filling the time with nothing and not asking yourself to feel anything.

quote.text: Grace fills empty spaces, but it can only enter where there is a void to receive it.
quote.author: Simone Weil

confusion.text: You can spend a whole hour over a geometry problem you never manage to solve — and Weil insisted that the hour was not wasted. When you are lost and want an answer right away, her thought sounds strange and unexpectedly comforting. In her essay on school studies, Simone Weil described attention in a special way. In her view, attention is not tension or a furrowed brow but the ability to suspend thought, leaving it free and open, ready to receive whatever comes. She compared it to solving a difficult geometry problem: the answer often appears not through pressure but through patient waiting. It follows that confusion is not a failure but a moment when the ready-made answers have run out. Instead of grabbing the first solution that turns up, you can stay with the question. Such waiting is not passivity but a special form of attention.
confusion.practice: Imagine your question as a geometry problem lying on the table in front of you. For three minutes just look at it without solving it — as Weil advised schoolchildren — and notice whether something surfaces on its own.

fatigue.text: When an apprentice gets hurt or complains of being tired, workers say, “It's the trade entering his body” — Weil wrote down this expression and loved it. Your exhaustion is real, and she knew it from the inside. A philosophy teacher, she went to work in a factory for a year to understand the lives of workers, and she described how exhausting, monotonous labor under time pressure crushes the very ability to think. She did not see this as a personal weakness of the workers: the problem lay in the conditions. In other words, burnout is not your personal failure but the result of being asked, for a long time, for more than a human being can bear. Weil also noticed that we often confuse attention with muscular strain. Real attention doesn't require clenched teeth. Perhaps what matters now is not to strain harder but to loosen your grip.
fatigue.practice: Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, smooth your forehead — Weil said attention does not live in clenched muscles. Do this slowly three times, releasing one place on each exhalation.

boredom.text: “Imaginary good is boring and flat; real good is always new, marvelous, intoxicating,” Weil wrote. When boredom drags on for hours, it is agonizing, but her paradox hints that what bores us may be not the world but the imaginary. Daydreams, fantasies, invented dramas seem vivid but quickly repeat themselves; reality, if you look at it attentively, is always new. Weil would probably say that boredom is not a sign that the world is poor but a sign that attention is tired of gliding over the surface. Weil taught an “attentive gaze”: looking at a thing, a person or a task so long and so openly that it begins to reveal itself. Boredom then is an invitation not to new entertainments but to a slower, deeper look at what is already near you.
boredom.practice: Take the most ordinary thing — a cup, a leaf, your own palm — and find ten details in it you hadn't noticed before, naming each one silently. This is the always-new reality Weil spoke of.

quote.text: Imaginary evil is romantic and varied; real evil is gloomy, monotonous, barren, boring. Imaginary good is boring; real good is always new, marvellous, intoxicating.
quote.author: Simone Weil

joy.text: At Solesmes, during Holy Week, Weil listened to Gregorian chant through a crushing headache — and found in that beauty “a pure and perfect joy.” Your joy is precious, and for all the rigor of her thought, Weil would take it very seriously. She wrote that joy and pain are equally precious gifts, and each deserves to be lived fully, in its purity, without mixing one with the other. For Weil, joy is connected with the beauty of the world and with a sense of reality: in joy we feel especially clearly that the world exists. In this light, your joy needs neither justifying nor “diluting” with worries that it will pass. You can simply be in it wholly, with attention. Attentive joy, for Weil, is no less deep than suffering — and no less true.
joy.practice: Stop for a minute and let the joy run through your whole body — from your face to your feet — adding nothing to it. Then say two simple words to yourself: “It is.”

love.text: “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity,” Weil wrote to her friend, the poet Joë Bousquet. The tenderness you feel now is, for her, inseparable from that kind of attention. To love, for her, means to see the other as they are, not as our imagination or our desires paint them. She wrote that love needs reality. Real attention means setting yourself aside for a while to make room for the other. This is not erasing yourself but generosity. Seen this way, your tenderness is not just a pleasant feeling but a particular way of looking: carefully, patiently, with interest in who this person really is. Such attention, for Weil, is a rare gift, and it can be given in the simplest things: in the way you listen.
love.practice: In your next conversation with someone close, give them one full minute — no advice, no stories of your own, only attention to what they're saying. This is generosity as Weil understood it.

quote.text: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
quote.author: Simone Weil

gratitude.text: In 1941 Weil worked in the grape harvest and recited the Lord's Prayer to herself in Greek — simply to hold her attention. The warm feeling of gratitude she understood as a response to a gift. She wrote a great deal about the beauty of the world as something given to us without any merit of our own. The sun shines on everyone, the rain falls for everyone; the world, in her view, is full of gifts we did not earn. For Weil, a believer, this was grace, but a non-religious reader can understand her thought too: much of what is good in life comes not as a reward but as a gift. For Weil, gratitude is attention to the gift. This is exactly what Weil taught — to see what is, clearly and openly — and gratitude becomes the natural response to such a gaze.
gratitude.practice: Step outside or open a window and find three things that came to you free today — light, air, someone's voice. Say a short “thank you” to each, silently.

hope.text: “Waiting patiently in expectation is the foundation of the spiritual life,” Weil wrote. In her language, your hope would be called just that: waiting. One of her books is called Waiting for God. For Weil, waiting is neither passive inaction nor an attempt to seize the future, but patient openness. She wrote that we receive the most precious things not when we chase them but when we know how to wait for them. It follows that hope is not a demand made of the future but an attentive readiness for what it may bring. Such hope doesn't break under delays, because it isn't tied to deadlines. It simply stays open. You can cherish your hope without clenching it in your fist.
hope.practice: On the in-breath silently name what you hope for; on the out-breath open your palms: “I wait without grasping.” Repeat five times — hope without a fist.

nostalgia.text: “The destruction of the past is perhaps the greatest of all crimes,” Weil wrote in The Need for Roots. Longing for the past is, for her, not a whim but the voice of one of our deepest needs. She believed that the past is one of the most vital needs of the human soul. We are nourished by what we have received from the past: from family, place, language, traditions. Weil wrote with alarm about how easily the past is destroyed and how hard it is to bring back. Seen this way, nostalgia is neither a weakness nor an escape from the present but a sign that the soul is looking for its roots. This doesn't mean you should live in the past. It means the past can be carefully kept as a source of nourishment — remembered not only with sadness but also with gratitude for what was.
nostalgia.practice: Take out one object from the past — a photo, a cup, something from home — and put it somewhere visible today. Let it be a metaxu, a bridge, as Weil called the things that connect us to our roots.

craving.text: “The great trouble in human life is that looking and eating are two different operations,” Weil observed. When a sharp craving comes over you, there is nothing shameful in it: it is a hunger looking for something to fill it. She wrote about “gravity” — the soul's natural drive to fill a void with something that brings quick relief. Weil also spoke of the soul's hunger: the danger is not that we are hungry but that we can mistake one thing for another. Weil would probably say that a craving often points to a real need — for calm, closeness, rest, meaning — which something is trying to replace. A craving comes in a wave: it rises and falls. You might try not to fight it but to look at it attentively: what hunger is hidden beneath it?
craving.practice: When the craving rises, picture it as a wave and simply watch it grow, crest and fall — doing nothing, only looking. Then ask: “What hunger is underneath it?”

addiction.text: Weil distrusted “clenched teeth”: the will, she believed, can move muscles but cannot summon what truly changes us. So for her, addiction would be neither a moral failure nor proof of weak character. She described the life of the soul through the image of gravity: habits and desires pull us down almost like a law of nature, and willpower alone is often not enough to resist them. Change, for Weil, comes through attention and through what doesn't depend on us alone — through help, an encounter, support from outside. Carrying Weil's thought further, addiction is often connected with being uprooted: a person lacks roots, bonds, a place among people. So the way out is not only an inner struggle but also rebuilding connections with others.
addiction.practice: Name to yourself one person or one community — a mutual-help group, for instance — where this can be talked about without judgment. Weil called such bonds roots; simply note that this root exists.

hangover.text: Weil wrote that we “read” the world like a text, and often read into it what isn't there. On the morning after, when your body aches and inside there's anxiety, shame and gaps in memory, that reading turns especially dark. She also noticed how imagination hurries to fill a void. For Weil, the gaps in last night are especially easily filled with the darkest pictures: “I must have said something terrible.” Instead of imagination, Weil proposed attention to reality: to what is actually known. You don't need to justify yourself or punish yourself. You can take care of the body that is suffering now, and let the gap in memory stay empty for the time being. Later, more calmly, you can find out what really happened — and then respond to reality rather than to fear.
hangover.practice: Sit by a window and slowly name aloud what you know for sure about last night — only facts, one at a time. When “I must have…” creeps in, answer: “That's imagination” — and return to the facts.

euphoria.text: “Beauty is a fruit we look at without trying to seize it,” Weil wrote: we want to look at what is beautiful, not to “eat” it. This burst is bright and alive right now, and there is no need to spoil it. Weil suggests that euphoria can be lived the same way — by contemplating it, not by trying to hold on to it by force. Trying to prolong the high at any cost is already “gravity,” reaching for compensation. Living it attentively, however, lets you take in this light without clinging to it. Euphoria is a moment when the world seems especially open. You can simply live it in all its fullness and notice what exactly is making you so glad right now.
euphoria.practice: Name three things that seem especially vivid right now, and look at each the way you'd look at a fruit you don't intend to pick. Don't try to prolong the moment.

crash.text: A stone thrown upward always falls — Weil saw in this not just physics but a precise image of the soul. A moment ago everything shone, and now it's heavy; a crash like this truly hurts. She described “gravity” as a natural law of the soul: whatever has risen tends to come down, just as objects fall. This is not a punishment and not proof that the high was a deception. It's simply how human nature works. It follows that the crash is not a failure but a manifestation of gravity, which shouldn't be taken as the truth about yourself or the world. Weil did not propose fighting it with effort; she spoke of patience, and of how what helps us rise is what comes of its own accord. You can give yourself time, without drawing conclusions at the lowest point.
crash.practice: Do one small, gentle thing for your body — make tea, step outside for five minutes — and tell yourself: “This is gravity after the rise; it will pass.” Draw no conclusions at the lowest point.

panic.text: Weil loved simple, solid things: the weight of a tool in the hand, the resistance of material, the floor under your feet. When panic hits — your heart pounding, not enough air, a sense that something irreversible is about to happen — it is terrifying. In a moment like this there's no need to think about philosophy. But Simone Weil has a thought that can help in a simple way: attention directed at something concrete and real brings us back into the world. She taught looking at things clearly and slowly. A wave of panic usually builds, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You can let it pass, holding on with your attention to what is near — the solid floor, an object in your hand, a sound. The heaviness of an object, its weight, its realness — all of this is support while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and hold something heavy — a mug, a book. Breathe out longer than you breathe in, and hold on with your attention to the weight in your palm until the wave begins to ebb.

dread.text: Weil did not wave away the question “what is all this for?”: she looked at the world without illusions and saw in it “necessity” — impersonal laws that don't ask what we want. When the sense of the abyss overwhelms you, her gaze may help in an unexpected way. But she also wrote that this necessity can be beautiful. Her example: the sea is no less beautiful to us because ships sometimes sink in it — the beauty of the world and its indifference to us cannot be separated. Weil would probably say that dread before the vastness of the world and wonder at it are two faces of one experience. You don't need to decide right now what the meaning of everything is. You can simply look at the sky, at a tree, and let yourself be part of this great world.
dread.practice: Go outside or to a window and find something that obeys necessity: clouds, wind, the lean of a tree. For a minute watch how it is beautiful and indifferent at once.

fomo.text: Weil could have quietly taught philosophy, yet she went to stand at a factory machine: she wanted not a picture of someone else's life but life itself. When it seems everyone else lives more interestingly, her choice is an unexpected hint. She set imagination against reality: imagination paints bright pictures full of life that turn out, in fact, to be mere fantasy. Carrying Weil's thought further, the fear of missing out is a gaze fixed on the imagined lives of others. Weil stressed that real life means taking part in what is real: in a particular place, with particular people, in a particular task. She called this rootedness. Your own life, even if it isn't so bright right now, is real. Bringing your attention back to it is not a consolation but a return to what actually is.
fomo.practice: Put your phone face down and name aloud three things that are real in your life right now: a place, a person, a task. Weil would call them roots.

sleepless.text: Suffering from headaches for years, Weil knew long nights when the body won't let go and sleep won't come. Lying awake at three in the morning alone with your thoughts is hard. At night, when nothing distracts you, imagination becomes especially loud. Simone Weil wrote that imagination hurries to fill any void — and the silence of the night looks to it like a void that needs to be occupied. For Weil, nighttime thoughts are not always the truth about your life but rather imagination at work in the dark. Instead, Weil proposed patient attention and waiting. You don't need to solve what is spinning in your head right now. You can simply lie in the quiet, without demanding that you fall asleep, and let the night be. Sometimes that is enough for the body to remember again how to rest.
sleepless.practice: Lay your palm on your chest and count your out-breaths from one to ten, then start again at one. Don't demand sleep of yourself — just wait, the way Weil taught waiting: openly, without pressure.

betrayal.text: In every human heart, Weil wrote, lives a child's cry: “Why am I being hurt?” When you've been betrayed, that cry is especially loud, and your pain is entirely legitimate. She also wrote about how painful it is to discover that we loved not the real person but an image created by our imagination. This doesn't mean you are to blame: trust is not a mistake but a way of loving. But the gap between the image and the reality can be agonizing. Weil suggests that betrayal is a painful encounter with the reality of another person, which turned out to be different from what you hoped. Weil did not demand that we quickly forgive or understand. She proposed looking at reality clearly, without turning away — and this, though painful, can gradually become something to stand on.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud, briefly and precisely, what exactly was broken: your image of the person, trust, shared plans. Weil valued the precise word over the comforting one; name it without judging yourself.

jealousy.text: “To love purely is to consent to distance,” Weil wrote: the other person is separate, free, and does not belong to us. When jealousy torments you, with its fear of losing and its urge to hold on, such consent seems almost impossible. She believed that the desire to possess another is a manifestation of “gravity,” not love in its pure form. It follows that jealousy is love mixed with the fear of loss. There's no need to be ashamed of it. But you can notice that in jealousy, attention is often turned toward imagined scenarios rather than toward the real person. Weil proposed returning to reality: what do you actually know, and what is fear filling in?
jealousy.practice: Picture the person you love at arm's length: separate, free, living their own life. Look at this picture for a minute and ask: which of my fears are reality, and which has imagination drawn in?

resentment.text: “And forgive us our debts” — Weil recited these words in Greek every day and saw in them something very hard. Old resentment is a heavy load, and it didn't come from nowhere: you really were hurt. She wrote about “the forgiveness of debts.” She meant that we often expect the past to give back what it owes us — an apology, justice, lost time. Weil considered this expectation very human, but also very heavy. In other words, resentment is a bill we keep presenting. For Weil, forgiving a debt is neither an obligation nor an excuse for the one who hurt you, but an acceptance that the past will not pay back what it took. This can free up room for the present. But there's no need to hurry: it happens when you are ready.
resentment.practice: Write down what you are “owed” in this situation: an apology, justice, time. Don't cancel the debt — just look straight at the bill, the way one looks at reality.

heartbreak.text: For Weil, in true love two people remain two: the other never becomes an extension of our desires. When a relationship has ended and your heart is broken, this thought sounds bitter, and the pain is among the sharpest there is — it deserves time and gentleness. She wrote about love as attention to the reality of another person. Weil said that imagination hurries to fill the void: with fantasies of how things could have been, with reproaches, with dreams of getting back together. Weil would probably say that these fantasies are understandable, but they prolong the pain. You can little by little bring your attention back to reality: to yourself, to your days, to what you received from this love. The void a person leaves behind can, in time, become a place for something new.
heartbreak.practice: Put away one thing that now feeds fantasies of getting back together — not throwing it out, just into a drawer. And name aloud one thing you received from this love and will keep.

impostor.text: At fourteen, Simone Weil was convinced that next to her brilliant mathematician brother she was a mediocrity shut out from truth. If you too feel you're about to be found out, her way out of that despair is worth hearing. Later, in her essay on school studies, she wrote that the value of an effort of attention doesn't depend on the result: even if the problem isn't solved, the attention put into it is not lost. She advised looking at your mistakes calmly and attentively, without self-abasement — as part of learning. Carrying Weil's thought further, impostor syndrome measures you against an imagined ideal. Weil proposed looking at reality instead: at what you actually do and what you are learning. Real effort, even imperfect, is not a fake. It is exactly what mastery grows from.
impostor.practice: Recall one recent mistake and tell yourself about it aloud, the way a teacher tells a student: what happened and what it taught you. Weil said this is how we learn — by looking at the mistake, not away.

self_hatred.text: Weil would ask not “what's wrong with you?” but “who hurt you?” — for severe pain, as she noticed, leaves a brand of self-contempt on the soul, as if the person were to blame for their own suffering. It is a very heavy feeling, and you don't have to accept its verdict. She saw in this the trace of a wound, not the truth about the person. Weil has the concept of “decreation,” which is sometimes misunderstood. Decreation is neither destruction nor self-hatred: Weil herself distinguished it from destruction. It is loosening the ego's grip to make room for attention to the world and to others. Seen this way, self-hatred is the opposite — an agonizing fixation on one's own image. You are allowed to treat yourself with the same gentleness you would show another person who is suffering.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine a close friend saying these words about themselves aloud. Answer them as you would — aloud or in a whisper — then repeat that answer, addressing yourself.

helplessness.text: Force, Weil wrote in her essay on the Iliad, turns a person into a thing — both the one who suffers it and the one who wields it. When you can change nothing, it is one of the hardest experiences, and she knew it well. She saw up close how factory workers were turned into appendages of machines, how war stripped people of all power over their fate. Weil did not say that helplessness is your fault. She saw it as a consequence of how the world and society are arranged. But she also stressed that even in helplessness the possibility of attention remains: to see clearly what is happening and not to turn away from others who suffer nearby. Weil suggests that attention is something that can't be taken away completely. It isn't omnipotence, but it isn't nothing either.
helplessness.practice: Choose one thing near you that no one can take away while you're looking at it: light on the wall, a sound outside, your own palm. Hold your attention on it for a minute — the small remnant of freedom Weil spoke of.

procrastination.text: A schoolboy frowns, holds his breath, tenses his muscles — and thinks that is attention; Weil would smile at the picture. If you can't get started, it's easy to blame yourself for laziness, but things are usually more complicated. In her essay on school studies she wrote that attention is not muscular strain. We often think we need to pull ourselves together, grit our teeth, and then it will work. But such strain, for Weil, tends to get in the way. Real attention is openness, almost a kind of waiting. It follows that procrastination is sometimes born of fear of the huge effort that seems necessary. Weil, however, advised treating work as an exercise: what matters is not the result but the attentive effort itself, even a small one. That way you can begin without demanding a lot of yourself all at once.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and do the smallest piece of the task the way you'd do a school exercise — with no aim of finishing. When it rings, you may stop.

uprooted.text: “To be rooted is perhaps the most important and least recognized need of the human soul,” Weil wrote. If you've been torn from home, that pain runs deep, and she devoted an entire book to it. She wrote The Need for Roots in London in 1943, a refugee herself, cut off from her native France. For Weil, rootedness is participation in the life of a community that preserves treasures of the past and expectations of the future: through place, language, work, people. She called the loss of roots one of the most dangerous diseases that can strike a person and a society. Seen this way, your pain is not a weakness but a response to the loss of one of the soul's deepest needs. Roots, for Weil, can also be put down anew: by taking part in the life of a new place, through habits, connections, work, language.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place for five minutes and choose one spot that will become “yours”: a bench, a tree, a bakery window. Greet it silently — that's how the first root goes down.

quote.text: To be rooted is perhaps the most important and least recognized need of the human soul.
quote.author: Simone Weil

overload.text: If Weil glanced at today's feed, she would probably recognize a factory assembly line — only for thoughts. The overload and the endless stream wear you out: attention splinters, and you can't focus on anything. For Simone Weil, attention was the most precious thing a person has. She wrote of it as the rarest form of generosity and almost as prayer. Working in a factory, she saw how the speed and monotony of labor destroy the ability to think. Weil would probably say that informational noise works in a similar way: attention torn into a thousand little pieces stops being attention. This is not your fault; these are the conditions we live in. But attention can gradually be gathered again: by directing it at one thing at a time, slowly and wholly.
overload.practice: Pour a cup of tea or water and give it all your attention for two minutes — color, warmth, the sound of swallowing — with your phone in another room. One thing, wholly: for Weil, that's how attention gathers itself again.

unreality.text: A piece of metal on a lathe doesn't argue or console — it simply resists, and Weil saw a lesson in reality there. If everything seems unreal right now, that can be frightening, and the feeling deserves gentle attention. For Simone Weil, “reality” was a key word. She believed that contact with reality happens above all through the body and through work: through the weight of an object, the resistance of material, the effort of muscles. It's no accident her book is called Gravity and Grace: for her, gravity is also the weight of the world, its realness. Carrying Weil's thought further, when the sense of reality is muted, what helps you return is not reflection but simple physical contact with the world. Things go on having weight and shape, even when everything inside feels far away.
unreality.practice: Press your palms against a wall or table and push — feel how the surface doesn't give. Stay with that resistance for five slow breaths.

awe.text: In the little chapel in Assisi where Francis prayed, Weil once felt something stronger than herself bring her to her knees. The awe you're feeling before something vast or beautiful was known to her — and she held it precious. For Simone Weil, the beauty of the world was one of the most direct paths to what is greater than us. She wrote that beauty is something we desire without trying to possess it: we want to look at what is beautiful, not own it. Weil saw in the beauty of the world an order and a necessity in which one can sense the harmony of the whole. For Weil, awe is pure attention that demands nothing. It is worth simply living it: letting yourself be small before something great — and there will be no humiliation in this, only joy.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what stirred your awe, phone put away — no photo, no search for words. Simply look, letting yourself be small.

relief.text: Weil set “gravity” against “grace”: gravity pulls down, while grace comes by itself, when we can no longer haul the load. Relief is like an exhale after long tension, and you can simply live it. And it sometimes resembles grace: it comes unexpectedly, when the load suddenly grows lighter. There's no need to immediately look for explanations or think about the next problem. Weil valued the ability to receive gifts without appropriating them. Relief is such a gift. You can pause and notice: what has changed in your body, your breathing, your gaze? This too is part of reality, and it deserves attention no less than the hard moments do.
relief.practice: Take three slow out-breaths, each longer than the last, and on the final one notice where your body has lightened. Stay with that place, not hurrying to the next worry.

calm.text: Weil learned George Herbert's poem “Love” by heart and recited it slowly, putting all her attention into each word — this was how she found stillness amid her headaches. The calm that has come to you now is precious and needs no justification. For Simone Weil, calm was connected with attention and waiting: the ability to be open without demanding anything. She wrote that attention, taken to its highest degree, becomes like prayer — for her, a believer, this was meant literally, but a non-religious reader can also sense what she means: a full, quiet openness to what is. It follows that calm is not the absence of life but a particular fullness of it. Weil also spoke of consent to necessity — to the way the world is. Calm can be that kind of consent: the world is as it is, and right now that is enough.
calm.practice: Sit in silence for a minute and note three things that simply are: a sound, the light, your breath. Do nothing with them — let calm be consent, not a task.

inspiration.text: “The poet produces the beautiful by fixing his attention on something real,” Weil wrote. Now, as new ideas and images arrive, her thought is especially timely. She wrote that we receive the most precious gifts not when we chase them but when we know how to wait for them. Attention, for her, is not strained effort but an open readiness to receive whatever comes. Seen this way, inspiration resembles grace: it comes by itself, but it comes to where there is room for it. Weil believed that this room is made by attention — patient, lengthy, sometimes seemingly fruitless. So inspiration is not an accident but a response to the openness you may have long been cultivating in yourself. It's worth catching while it's fresh.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down right now, as it is, without correcting it — while it's fresh. Then for a minute look at something real nearby that it may have grown from.

schadenfreude.text: Weil was drawing up something like a physics of the soul: as water flows downhill, suffering looks for somewhere to unload itself. Schadenfreude is a shameful feeling, but she probably wouldn't judge you for it. In Gravity and Grace she described a law resembling a physical one: a suffering person tries somehow to lessen their suffering — for instance, by passing it outward or by feeling that they are not the only one down below. She attributed all this to “gravity” — a natural movement of the soul that happens on its own, without our choosing. Weil would probably say that schadenfreude often reveals not malice but one's own accumulated pain: someone else's failure balances the scales for a moment. Weil did not propose fighting gravity by force. She proposed attention: seeing what is happening inside without turning away — and then the feeling itself already begins to change.
schadenfreude.practice: Put a hand on your solar plexus and quietly ask: “Which pain of mine felt lighter for a moment at someone else's failure?” Name it in one word — and wish that person something good, however small.

contempt.text: The Samaritan stopped beside a beaten stranger on the road — Weil called that kind of gaze “creative attention”: it sees a person where others walk past. Contempt, by contrast, comes easily — toward those who seem stupid, weak or unworthy. She thought a great deal about how people stop seeing one another as human. Carrying Weil's thought further, contempt is a small form of the force that turns a person into a thing: in our gaze, another person turns from someone alive into “a nobody.” The opposite of this, for Weil, is attention: the ability to see the real person, not an image created by our irritation. This doesn't require agreeing with them or approving of what they do. But attention restores fullness to both you and them — and often shows that behind the contempt there was tiredness or hurt.
contempt.practice: Think of the person you despise and imagine their morning: how they wake, what they eat, whom they worry about. Name to yourself one real detail of their life — without judgment.

disgust.text: Weil knew a world few philosophers have seen from the inside: in her Factory Journal she described the oil, the din and the grime of the shop floor without squeamishness and without embellishment. Disgust — at people, a situation, sometimes yourself — is a strong bodily feeling, and it isn't chosen. Her central idea is attention: looking at reality as it is, without replacing it with what imagination paints. For Weil, disgust often concerns not the thing itself but the image we have built around it. Weil did not demand suppressing this feeling. She suggested letting your gaze linger a little longer than you want to — and then, in what repels you, something simply human, fragile, in need, sometimes shows through.
disgust.practice: Describe aloud what disgusts you in three neutral words, the way Weil would in her factory journal: color, shape, sound. Notice whether the feeling's strength has changed.

revenge.text: Weil fought injustice all her life — and yet refused to answer evil with evil. The wish for revenge is a natural response to harm done to you, and she understood its mechanics well. In Gravity and Grace she described how a person who has been hurt tends to pass the pain on, as though that would restore a broken balance. She attributed this to “gravity”: a movement of the soul that happens almost by itself, like an object falling. But Weil believed it is possible not to be a mere transmitter of evil. Her image is of a person in whom evil stops instead of continuing. This does not mean staying silent about what happened or agreeing with it: Weil herself never kept silent about injustice. It means giving up only one thing — the wish for the other person to suffer in the same way.
revenge.practice: Say aloud what you actually need right now: acknowledgment, protection, justice, peace? Choose one you could reach without harming anyone, and note the first small step.

anger_at_loved.text: Each of us, for Weil, carries portraits of our loved ones in our head — and sometimes loves and expects the portrait more than the living person. Anger at a partner, parents or children is inevitable, because they are the people we live closest to. A person close to us inevitably doesn't match our picture, and irritation is born of that mismatch. It follows that anger at loved ones is often anger at the gap between the imagined and the real. Weil called attention to the real person one of the hardest forms of love. This doesn't mean the anger is wrong: sometimes it points to a real injustice. But the shame after an outburst doesn't have to become a punishment. It's better to ask: whom did I just see — a living person, or my picture of them?
anger_at_loved.practice: Look at your loved one (or their photo) for a minute as if seeing them for the first time: a wrinkle, a gesture, tiredness. Ask yourself: whom am I seeing now — them, or my picture of them?

ambivalence.text: “Contradiction is the lever of transcendence” — one of Weil's most enigmatic formulas. To love someone and at the same time be unable to stand them is a heavy but honest state. She valued contradictions and believed there's no need to hurry to resolve them. In Gravity and Grace she wrote that when the mind runs up against a contradiction that cannot be removed, it can become something like a lever — a way of seeing reality more deeply. In other words, mixed feelings toward someone close are neither a mistake nor a sign of poor love. They are a sign that you see the person whole, not as a convenient image. Imagination wants to simplify everything: either they are good or they are bad. Attention allows you to hold both feelings at once, crossing out neither. A love that contains both tenderness and irritation is not lesser but truer.
ambivalence.practice: Say one sentence aloud: “I love in you… and I find it hard with your…”, filling in both parts. Don't choose between them — just listen to how they sound together.

guilty_relief.text: Weil noticed that “affliction” — a mixture of suffering, powerlessness and loneliness — weighs not only on the one who suffers but on everyone nearby. The relief when that burden lifts — after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time — is often hidden even from ourselves. Caring for such a person, or living alongside long-lasting pain, means carrying a very heavy load for years. Weil would probably say that relief is the natural response of a soul from which a weight has been lifted. It does not mean you loved less. Weil distinguished reality from imagination: imagination paints a picture in which the “right” kind of person should feel only grief. Reality is more complicated: love and relief can exist in you at the same time, and neither cancels the other.
guilty_relief.practice: Sit by a window and quietly say: “I feel lighter. And I loved.” Sit for a minute with these two sentences side by side, adding nothing.

indifference.text: After factory shifts, Weil admitted she had no strength left to think or to feel — she knew numbness from the inside. If where something “should” move you there is only blankness, and worry about yourself joins it, that is hard. She wrote about “affliction” and showed that intense suffering can cause numbness: the soul seems to stop feeling in order to endure. Carrying Weil's thought further, indifference doesn't necessarily mean callousness. Sometimes it's tiredness, sometimes protection, sometimes simply a pause. Weil valued honesty before reality more than a display of the right feelings. If right now you don't feel what you're “supposed” to, you can admit it without shame. Attention, for Weil, doesn't require emotions — you can look at a person or an event honestly, without strong feelings.
indifference.practice: Look for a minute at what “should” move you, the way you'd look at a problem you're not obliged to solve — attentively, demanding no feelings of yourself.

escape.text: In 1934 Weil took leave from her lycée and went onto the shop floor: a philosophy teacher became a worker at the Alsthom factory. The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — she, who changed places and occupations more than once, would probably understand from the inside. In The Need for Roots she described the needs of the soul, and among them are not only order and rootedness but also the need for risk, for liberty, for responsibility. When life becomes monotonous and devoid of meaning, the soul, for Weil, suffers from it the way a body suffers from hunger. For Weil, the desire to escape is a signal of an unmet need, not a whim. But Weil also warned of “compensations” — imaginary worlds the soul flees to from reality. It's worth asking attentively: what exactly am I missing — and is there room for it here?
escape.practice: Imagine for a minute that you've already left: what feeling comes first — freedom, risk, calm, respect? Name that word and look for where in your present life it could have even a small place.

forbidden_attraction.text: Weil the Platonist loved an image from the Phaedrus: at the sight of beauty the soul's wings begin to grow again, and it is sweet and painful at once. Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” can be just as strong and tangled. She wrote a great deal about desire and did not consider it trivial: in it she saw the soul's pull toward goodness and beauty, even if aimed somewhere other than we expect. Weil suggests that attraction shows what fullness, beauty or aliveness your soul is reaching for. Weil gave no ready-made answers about what to do with desire. She suggested first looking — attentively and honestly, without filling in the picture with imagination. Sometimes behind an attraction to a particular person lies a thirst for a quality of life you are missing.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Take a five-minute walk and ask yourself, without naming the person: “What quality of life do I feel near this attraction — aliveness, tenderness, freedom, risk?” Look along the way for where it exists in your own life.

quote.text: The great trouble in human life is that looking and eating are two different operations.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Forms of the Implicit Love of God,” in Waiting for God

social_anxiety.text: On the factory floor Weil was the clumsiest of workers: things kept slipping from her hands, and she felt people's eyes on her keenly. Fear of people and their judgment can freeze you and drain your strength — she knew it well. Shy by nature, she often felt like an outsider both in academic circles and in the factory. Attention, for Weil, is turned away from oneself — toward reality, toward another person. Social anxiety, by contrast, turns the gaze inward: how do I look, what will they think of me. It follows that relief comes not from being liked but from forgetting yourself a little by becoming genuinely interested in the other person. Try shifting your attention to the person beside you — not to come across better, but simply out of curiosity about them.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, ask the other person one sincere question about themselves and hear the answer through. Notice where your anxiety goes meanwhile.

uncertainty.text: “What if you simply don't know?” Weil would ask this seriously: she valued honest not-knowing above an invented answer. When nothing is clear it's hard: the mind wants to fill the void with an answer, even a frightening one. She wrote that imagination strives to “fill the void” — and then we invent scenarios that seem more real than reality itself. Weil proposed another path — attention: the ability not to grab the first thought, to stay open and wait until reality reveals itself. In other words, uncertainty is a space that doesn't have to be filled with anxious pictures. You can admit, “I don't know” — and stay in that not-knowing a little longer, without turning away from it.
uncertainty.practice: When your mind starts drawing scenarios, tell it calmly: “That's imagination. I don't know.” Repeat these phrases slowly, in step with your walking, as you pace the room for a couple of minutes.

quote.text: Attention consists of suspending our thought, leaving it detached, empty, and ready to be penetrated by the object.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

waiting.text: At the factory, what wore Weil down most were the minutes waiting for the setter or an order, when nothing depended on her. Waiting for an answer, results, news can be agonizing. But for Simone Weil, waiting was not an empty waste of time but one of the soul's central states. Her posthumous collection is called Waiting for God, and in her essay on school studies she wrote that what is most valuable cannot be seized by effort — it can only be waited for, attentively. Weil distinguished tense, impatient waiting, which wears you out, from patient, open waiting, in which a person doesn't cling to a particular outcome. Weil would probably say that waiting is agonizing as long as imagination paints answers in place of reality. But it can be lived differently — as a pause in which you are attentive to what is here now.
waiting.practice: When you feel the urge to check whether the answer has come, take three slow breaths and name one thing you can hear right now. Only then check.

quote.text: We do not obtain the most precious gifts by going in search of them but by waiting for them.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

regret.text: “What would a good teacher do with this mistake?” Weil, who taught for years herself, would probably start with that question. Regret over what you did or didn't do can hold on for a long time, and there is honest pain in it. She had deep respect for reality, including the past: what has happened is already part of the world and can't be rewritten. But she distinguished two attitudes toward mistakes. One is tormenting self-accusation, which in essence still revolves around the “I.” The other is attention: a calm, honest look at what happened, with no attempt either to justify or to punish yourself. Carrying Weil's thought further, regret is valuable when it becomes knowledge rather than punishment. The past can't be changed, but you can understand what it teaches — and that knowledge already changes the present.
regret.practice: Choose one small action in which the lesson of this mistake can be applied today — and do it. That, for Weil, is how regret becomes knowledge.

longing.text: Two prisoners in neighboring cells tap messages through the wall: the wall separates them — and it is also what lets them speak. This is how Weil thought about separation from someone you love, and what you feel now is exactly the pain in which love shows most clearly. She wrote about love for someone absent, about how hard it is to bear the void left in the other's place. The soul strives to fill it: with imagined conversations, fantasies of meeting, reproaches. Weil called such fillers “compensations” and did not condemn them, but suggested sometimes leaving the place empty — not out of asceticism, but out of respect for reality. For Weil, longing is love that for now cannot show itself in presence. It can be lived not as a lack but as a special form of faithfulness to someone dear to you.
longing.practice: Tap your fingers on the table a few times — like a prisoner sending word through the wall — and recall one real detail of this person: a gesture, an intonation. Stay with it for a minute without turning it into a fantasy.

world_pain.text: At six, Simone Weil gave up sugar on learning that the soldiers at the front had none, and as an adult she went into a factory to share the lives of workers. Pain for the world — wars, injustice, the suffering of people you'll never meet — she felt all her life, and she knew how vast it can be. Her main answer to others' suffering is attention. She believed that true love of one's neighbor begins by simply seeing a person in trouble and asking what they are going through. Weil's answer would be: you cannot hold all the pain of the world, but you can truly see at least one person who is struggling. This small form of attention is not an escape from the great pain but an honest, doable response to it.
world_pain.practice: Call or send word today to one real person who is having a hard time — near or far. Ask how they are and listen without advising.

quote.text: The love of our neighbor in all its fullness simply means being able to say to him: “What are you going through?”
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

rejection.text: Weil longed to be sent into occupied France, but in London her plan was politely turned down, and de Gaulle reportedly called her mad. Being rejected — as if you went unnoticed or were deemed unnecessary — hurts. She knew it before, too: she was not always taken seriously — not in academic circles, not in political movements, not among the workers, to whom she seemed strange. Most people, Weil wrote, look at others through imagination — they see their own expectations, not the real person. It follows that rejection often speaks of what the other person failed or didn't have time to see, not of your worth. That doesn't make it less painful. But you can acknowledge the pain without agreeing with the conclusion that you are worthless. The reality of you is larger than someone else's passing glance.
rejection.practice: Go to a mirror or a window and quietly name one thing in yourself worth being seen — honestly, without exaggeration. Weil would say this is the attention to reality the other person didn't manage.

abandonment.text: Metaxu — Greek for “intermediaries” — was Weil's name for everything that holds us in the world like bridges: home, language, friends, work. The fear of being abandoned is one of the oldest fears, and it strikes precisely at those bridges. She also wrote about “roots”: a person needs to be part of a community that preserves something of the past and expects something of the future. In other words, the fear of abandonment is the fear of losing roots, connection, support. Weil did not propose getting rid of this need. She said that roots grow from many connections: people, place, work, language, a shared cause, tradition. When there are roots in different places, the loss of one connection doesn't bring everything down. The fear can be softened by tending to your roots rather than clinging to one person.
abandonment.practice: Draw a small tree and label its roots: the people, places and activities that hold you. Mark one root that deserves some attention this week.

unrequited.text: Weil claimed something strange: love that receives nothing in return does not thereby become less real. When love goes unanswered, it wounds deeply, because love longs for meeting. She wrote about love in a very unexpected way: she believed that pure love includes consent to the distance between yourself and the one you love. For her this is not a renunciation of feeling but a recognition of the other's freedom and reality. The beloved is not an extension of our desires but a separate world. Weil would probably say that unrequited love is painful precisely because the distance is imposed, not chosen. Weil did not propose forcing yourself to “let go.” But she showed that even without an answer, your love could have been genuine — attention to a real person. That capacity stays with you, and the fact that it went unanswered doesn't cancel it.
unrequited.practice: Write on a slip of paper three things you saw in this person that were truly theirs, not your fantasy. Fold it and set it aside — let them simply be.

quote.text: To love purely is to consent to distance, it is to adore the distance between ourselves and that which we love.
quote.author: Simone Weil

humiliation.text: After the factory, Weil wrote that she had received there “the mark of a slave,” like the red-hot brand the Romans put on their most despised slaves. Humiliation wounds more deeply than many other feelings, and she knew it from the inside. In the factory she experienced firsthand how foremen treated workers, and wrote that her very sense of her own dignity was almost erased there. In The Need for Roots she named honor as one of the basic needs of the soul, and she included social humiliation in her notion of “affliction” — alongside pain and loneliness. Weil stressed that humiliation speaks of the force that was applied to a person, not of their worth. With Weil, you can acknowledge the full weight of humiliation — and refuse to believe what it tries to tell you about yourself.
humiliation.practice: Stand up, straighten your shoulders and slowly lift your chin — Weil held honor to be a need of the soul. Stand like this for five breaths and say to yourself: “I was treated badly, but I am not a thing.”

quote.text: Those who are unhappy have no need for anything in this world but people capable of giving them their attention.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

body_shame.text: Weil was known for her indifference to mirrors: she cared about what a body can do, not how it looks. If you're unhappy with your body, the feeling is often born of comparison with images. She distinguished reality from imagination: imagination, she said, constantly paints pictures that seem brighter and more “correct” than what is real. We look at the body not with our own eyes but with the eyes of an imagined judge, and compare it with images that don't exist in reality. For Weil, the body was first of all something that works, gets tired, feels, touches the world. For Weil, attention to the real body — not to a picture, but to what it does and feels — weakens the power of the imagined model. The body doesn't have to match an image to be part of the world.
body_shame.practice: Rest your palm on the part of your body you criticize and say one “thank you” to it for a specific job it does for you every day.

illness.text: “The capacity to give one's attention to a sufferer is a very rare and difficult thing; it is almost a miracle,” Weil wrote. When the body lets you down, illness changes everything: plans, strength, your very sense of yourself. For many years she herself lived with severe, exhausting headaches that kept her from working and thinking. She wrote about “affliction” — a state in which physical pain joins with loneliness and the feeling that no one is interested in you anymore. Weil stressed that such suffering is hard to see from the outside: people look away. That is why attention is so valuable — both from others and your own toward yourself. Weil suggests that illness doesn't make you less, even when it takes away your strength. She proposed not turning away: acknowledging the weight, and giving yourself and others the chance to be near it.
illness.practice: Send one person a short, honest message today about how you feel — without the automatic “I'm fine.” Letting someone be near you is attention too.

pride.text: Weil dreamed that every worker could at least once see the finished machine his part had gone into. What you feel now is a healthy pride in what you've done, and it is deserved. She was wary of the “I,” yet she highly valued the joy of work well done. Working in the factory, she saw how workers were deprived of this joy: they never saw the result of their labor and didn't understand what their part was for. It follows that healthy pride is not superiority over others but joy in touching reality through your own effort and attention. You made something, and the world is a little different because of you. You can quietly and honestly be glad of this — without apologizing and without comparing.
pride.practice: Look at what you've made for one minute — attentively, as if it were someone else's work — and name aloud one detail that came out well.

melancholy.text: “Distance is the soul of the beautiful,” Weil wrote in Gravity and Grace. That quiet state in which sadness joins something tender and clear lives precisely at this distance. She wrote about the beauty of the world and about how beauty is always a little sad: it can't be possessed, held on to or eaten — it can only be looked at. It is this distance, for Weil, that makes beauty pure. In other words, melancholy is a feeling in which we experience the impossibility of possessing what we love: a sunset, the past, a moment. It is neither an illness nor a weakness but a special sensitivity to the fragility of the world. She saw in it a seed of attention: the ability to look without demanding anything. Gentle sadness can simply be lived — as quiet contemplation of what is passing.
melancholy.practice: Read Weil's line slowly to yourself, twice: “Distance is the soul of the beautiful.” Then find one beautiful thing nearby and look at it for a minute, wanting nothing from it.
